extracted_by: hand, T-0261 — the Chicago American read, June to August 1835
note: Volume I, Number 9. Two claims here that nothing else in the run supplies: a THREE STOREY store rented for an auction room, and a school advertising an eleven-week term with a fee scale down to Latin and French. A third attorney (S. Abell) sets up doing land conveyancing, and the Marine Journal covers July 24-30. The tailor's street disagrees with the previous issue's and the disagreement is recorded, not resolved.

claims.normalized: Auction & Commission. [TH]E subscriber [in]form[s his cus]to[mers …] he has rented the three story st[ore] o[n] [uncertain: IWarpom' — a street name this column does not resolve] street, for the purpo[s]e [of] auction[eering …] Auctionee[r …] [uncertain: lo. Ly] street.
claims.notes: A THREE STOREY BUILDING IN CHICAGO, ONE MONTH AFTER THE SCENE DATE — and nothing else in this corpus documents a building of more than one storey by its own count. That matters to a reconstruction whose commercial frontage is built almost entirely from inference about height: here is a store big enough to be advertised BY its three storeys, rented whole as an auction room. TWO STREET NAMES ARE PRINTED AND NEITHER IS READ. 'IWarpom' stroet' matches no Chicago street this project holds — Water, Warren and Wabash have all been considered and none accounts for the characters — and the second, 'lo. Ly atreet', is worse. Both stay inside `[uncertain: …]`, because a three-storey building is exactly the kind of thing that would get built on the strength of a guessed address and then be wrong. The auctioneer is very probably W. Montgomery, who has taken two South Water Street stores in the previous month, but the signature here is destroyed and no attribution is made.

claims.notes: A SCHOOL WITH A PUBLISHED FEE SCALE, one month after the scene date — an eleven-week term, ordinary English branches at the bottom, higher branches at eleven dollars and Latin and French at eight. Read alongside the two school-district meetings this run documents (District 4 meeting in the Presbyterian Church to consider BUILDING a school-house, District 2 in the Baptist Meeting House), it says what schooling in Chicago actually was in 1835: private, subscription-funded and housed in whatever building would take it, with the public school-house still a proposal. NEITHER THE TEACHER'S NAME NOR THE PREMISES SURVIVE in this printing, so no business is recorded and no building is placed. The dollar figures are read from '81100' and '88,00', which is the OCR's usual treatment of a dollar sign, and they are bracketed.

claims.notes: THE PORT COLUMN FOR THE LAST WEEK OF JULY, and the shape of the trade has not changed since the scene date: the same hulls — Llewelling, Swan, Hiram, Jesse Smith, the steamboat Michigan — plus two new arrivals, the brigs Indiana and the schooner Commerce, both from Buffalo with merchandize. Milwaukee, Green Bay, St. Joseph and Buffalo are the four destinations again. Taken with the three earlier columns this project now has SIX WEEKS of continuous shipping either side of 1835-07-01, which is enough to say with confidence how many vessels were in the river on an ordinary day and what they were carrying.

claims.normalized: [NEW FA]SHION[A]BLE [Tailoring Establishment. The subscriber … h]a[s] [taken a] Shop in [uncertain: Laks runlie — a street name this printing does not resolve] […] beg[s] leave most re[spectfully to tender his services …]

business.name: a new tailoring establishment, Chicago, June 1835

claims.notes: THE TAILOR'S STREET, FOR THE THIRD TIME, AND THE THREE PRINTINGS DO NOT AGREE. 1835-06-27 reads 'Shop in Frank eter street'; 1835-07-25 reads 'Shop in rroklia', which that claim took as Franklin and recorded on the business; this one reads 'Shop in Laks runlie', whose first word is much closer to LAKE than to Franklin. So the corpus now supports Franklin on one printing, something Lake-shaped on another, and a broken fragment on the third — and this claim therefore records NO street and leaves the business's Franklin Street entry standing from the 07-25 witness with this disagreement written down beside it. A page-image pass should settle it before a tailor's shop is put anywhere. The honest summary is that one of the three readings is wrong and the transcription cannot say which.

claims.notes: THE STORY BEHIND THE FRAGMENT 1835-07-25 COULD NOT FINISH: a man who left Alabama for west Tennessee six or eight years earlier and died there, whose widow and children then moved to Indiana destitute, and whose relative in Courtland, Alabama is advertising across the western press to find them. It is quoted at length because it is the only extended piece of ordinary human circumstance in this run that is not a trade card, a meeting notice or a cargo list — the American's readership is a migrant population and this is what its notices column was for. The advertiser is in Alabama and NO Chicago resident is minted from it; the person recorded carries Courtland, Alabama as his place, which is what the notice says.
